source.title: The Architecture of Orientation
source.scope: Initial bounded pilot; not a representation of the entire manuscript

claims.statement: Orientation is a temporally extended relation among an agent, a world as disclosed to that agent, and a repertoire of possible action; it is not merely an internal representation.
claims.strongestCase: Purely representational accounts underdescribe embodied skill, norm-governed action, temporal identity, and the way a changed environment changes what can be done without first changing an explicit belief.
claims.counterclaim: Orientation can be modelled adequately as an internal state-estimation and policy-selection architecture; adding a constitutive agent-world relation may be redescriptive rather than explanatory.
confidenceReducers: A representational model predicts all alleged relational effects without ad hoc additions.
The proposed dimensions cannot be operationally distinguished from one another.
The definition expands whenever counterexamples arise and therefore excludes nothing.

challenge.statement: Specify a case in which the relational definition changes a prediction, classification, or intervention compared with a sufficiently rich internalist model.
challenge.requiredResponse: A discriminating case, not a restatement of relational vocabulary.

thirdOrderAudit.makesLegible: The joint dependence of action on agent, disclosed environment, history, and norms.
thirdOrderAudit.maySuppress: Mechanistic decomposition inside the agent and cases where internal representation is the most useful level.
thirdOrderAudit.authorityEffect: Privileges integrative interpreters who can redescribe multiple levels in one vocabulary.
thirdOrderAudit.subtractionCondition: Retire the constitutive reading if relational language adds no discriminating consequence across well-specified cases.

claims.statement: Attention partly determines which features and affordances of a situation become available for perception, interpretation, and action.
claims.primaryQuestion: By what mechanism is an actionable world disclosed?
claims.strongestCase: Attentional manipulations alter detection, salience, action preparation, and experienced relevance even when the external stimulus remains constant.
claims.counterclaim: Much salience is bottom-up, affective, habitual, or action-generated; attention may select after affordances have already been specified rather than disclose them.
confidenceReducers: Effects disappear when expectation, arousal, motor preparation, and demand characteristics are controlled.
Competing attentional taxonomies fail to map onto distinguishable disclosure profiles.
The claim predicts no more than the truism that selective processing is selective.
evidenceRequests: Experiments separating attention from expectation and motor preparation.
Within-person interventions showing changed actionable affordances under stable stimuli.
A taxonomy comparison using McGilchrist's proposed modes as hypotheses, not authorities.

challenge.statement: Distinguish attention changing perceptual availability from attention merely changing report, confidence, or response threshold.
challenge.requiredResponse: Pre-registered discriminants across at least two rival mechanisms.

thirdOrderAudit.makesLegible: Selective disclosure and its downstream action consequences.
thirdOrderAudit.maySuppress: Bottom-up capture, affect, interoception, motor exploration, and social cueing.
thirdOrderAudit.authorityEffect: Can let a preferred theory of attention define which worlds count as well perceived.
thirdOrderAudit.rivalPreserved: Affordances are specified pre-attentively and attention mainly governs access or report.
thirdOrderAudit.subtractionCondition: Narrow the claim to access or report if perceptual availability cannot be independently demonstrated.

claims.statement: Holding anomaly magnitude constant, anomalies that threaten identity-central commitments tend to produce disproportionately large defensive, destabilizing, or reorganizing responses.
claims.primaryQuestion: Why do some anomalies destabilize orientation more than others?
claims.strongestCase: Beliefs embedded in belonging, status, vocation, and moral identity have wider dependency networks and higher revision costs than isolated factual beliefs.
claims.counterclaim: Apparently identity-driven defence may be better explained by material interest, coalition pressure, reputational incentives, trauma, or asymmetric information.
confidenceReducers: Identity centrality adds no predictive value after incentives and social sanctions are measured.
The response curve is linear rather than thresholded or discontinuous.
The construct labels disagreement as pathology and cannot classify calm but strategic resistance.
evidenceRequests: Longitudinal measures separating identity centrality from confidence and material stake.
Cases of identity-central revision without defence and peripheral anomaly with strong defence.

challenge.statement: Demonstrate incremental prediction beyond incentives, coalition signalling, prior confidence, and perceived source hostility.
challenge.requiredResponse: A multilevel longitudinal or experimental design with rival predictors.

thirdOrderAudit.makesLegible: Revision costs created by identity dependencies.
thirdOrderAudit.maySuppress: Rational resistance, genuine persecution, material interests, and strategic behaviour.
thirdOrderAudit.authorityEffect: Can license interpreters to psychologize dissent.
thirdOrderAudit.rivalPreserved: Resistance is a rational response to incentives or hostile institutions.
thirdOrderAudit.subtractionCondition: Reject identity centrality as the dominant explanation where rival variables absorb its predictive contribution.

claims.statement: Experienced meaningfulness, coherence, purpose, or existential integration does not by itself establish the truth or ethical warrant of the orientation that produces it.
claims.primaryQuestion: What follows epistemically from experienced meaning?
claims.strongestCase: Fanaticism, delusion, exploitation, and mutually incompatible worldviews can each generate coherence and purpose.
claims.counterclaim: Durable, integrative meaningfulness across persons and time may be defeasible evidence of fit with reality even if it is not conclusive warrant.
confidenceReducers: A carefully specified form of meaning reliably predicts truth-conducive correction after confounds are controlled.
The distinction treats all first-person evidence as epistemically inert.

challenge.statement: Separate the denial of entailment from the stronger and unwarranted claim that meaning provides no evidence at all.
challenge.requiredResponse: A graded evidential account rather than a binary exclusion.

thirdOrderAudit.makesLegible: The gap between existential success and epistemic or moral success.
thirdOrderAudit.maySuppress: First-person evidence and the possibility that long-run integration is weak evidence of world-fit.
thirdOrderAudit.authorityEffect: May privilege external evaluators over participants' experience.
thirdOrderAudit.rivalPreserved: Some forms of durable meaning are defeasible evidence, though never guarantees.
thirdOrderAudit.subtractionCondition: Revise the categorical wording if particular meaning profiles show robust independent evidential value.

claims.statement: Other things equal, an orientation is better when it can receive, verify, integrate, enact, retain, and continue monitoring relevant correction without destroying the agency needed to learn.
claims.primaryQuestion: What makes an orientation better rather than merely stable or meaningful?
claims.strongestCase: Fallible agents and institutions need error-correction; systems that suppress feedback become brittle, captured, or delusional.
claims.counterclaim: Unbounded revisability can dissolve commitment, expertise, trust, and coordinated action; some closure is a precondition for agency.
confidenceReducers: Corrigibility cannot be distinguished from conformity to the evaluator's preferred evidence regime.
High-performing systems require forms of closure the proposal classifies as defects.
Correction burdens fall systematically on less powerful participants.

challenge.statement: Define optimal rather than maximal corrigibility and identify legitimate closure, decision deadlines, and asymmetric correction costs.
challenge.requiredResponse: A governance model with affected-party standing and stopping conditions.

thirdOrderAudit.makesLegible: Where correction pipelines fail between feedback and retained institutional learning.
thirdOrderAudit.maySuppress: The value of commitment, ritual stability, confidentiality, expertise, and timely closure.
thirdOrderAudit.authorityEffect: Whoever defines valid correction can govern the system's reality.
thirdOrderAudit.rivalPreserved: Reliable orientation requires bounded closure as well as openness.
thirdOrderAudit.subtractionCondition: Reject any universal maximization rule; retain only context-sensitive corrigibility if stability-correction trade-offs are irreducible.

claims.statement: Across bounded and independently coded corpora, myths may exhibit recurrent families of transformations concerning order, anomaly, disintegration, exploration, sacrifice, death, and renewal that exceed specified null models.
claims.primaryQuestion: What, if anything, recurs across myths?
claims.strongestCase: Human developmental constraints and recurrent coordination problems plausibly produce cross-cultural similarities at the level of transformations rather than exact plots or symbols.
claims.counterclaim: Apparent invariants are products of diffusion, translation, archive bias, flexible coding, or abstractions broad enough to fit nearly any narrative.
confidenceReducers: Preregistered coders cannot achieve reliability without knowing the hypothesis.
Null corpora and shuffled narratives exhibit the same invariants.
The proposed family fails out-of-sample on underrepresented traditions.
Diffusion and common source history account for the recurrence.
evidenceRequests: Preregistered corpus inclusion and transformation coding.
Null models, negative controls, diffusion controls, and out-of-sample tests.

challenge.statement: State the invariants before inspecting the test corpus and show that they discriminate myths from generic narrative structure.
challenge.requiredResponse: A replicable codebook, null model, and held-out corpus.

thirdOrderAudit.makesLegible: Recurrent narrative transformations that may organize orientation.
thirdOrderAudit.maySuppress: Local meanings, historical discontinuities, genre differences, and traditions excluded from surviving archives.
thirdOrderAudit.authorityEffect: Comparativists may overwrite participant interpretations with a universal schema.
thirdOrderAudit.rivalPreserved: Recurrence is mainly diffusion plus generic narrative compression.
thirdOrderAudit.subtractionCondition: Retire any proposed invariant that fails preregistered out-of-sample discrimination.

claims.statement: A candidate moral judgement gains credibility when it remains defensible under explicitly defined transformations of perspective, role, time, information, and affected-party position, although such invariance is neither sufficient nor self-interpreting.
claims.primaryQuestion: What shape might warranted moral judgement have across frames?
claims.strongestCase: Role reversal, temporal consistency, informed consent, and affected-party inclusion expose special pleading and frame-dependent domination.
claims.counterclaim: The selected transformations already encode substantive morality, while some genuine duties are role-asymmetric and should not be invariant.
confidenceReducers: Different defensible transformation sets rank the same judgement oppositely.
The proposal cannot accommodate legitimate partiality or asymmetric obligation.
Invariance merely redescribes reflective equilibrium without adding discipline.

challenge.statement: Specify which transformations preserve moral relevance and justify that selection without circularly assuming the desired result.
challenge.requiredResponse: A transformation ledger and adversarial examples involving legitimate asymmetry.

thirdOrderAudit.makesLegible: Special pleading, excluded perspectives, and unstable moral reasons.
thirdOrderAudit.maySuppress: Role-specific duties, historical repair, intimacy, and morally relevant asymmetry.
thirdOrderAudit.authorityEffect: The designer of admissible transformations can predetermine apparent invariance.
thirdOrderAudit.rivalPreserved: Pluralist reflective equilibrium without an invariance criterion.
thirdOrderAudit.subtractionCondition: Reduce the proposal to a limited diagnostic if no non-circular transformation set can be defended.

claims.statement: Christian Logos metaphysics can be explored as an interpretation of why truth, self-giving correction, reconciliation, and renewed order might belong together; mythology or psychological recurrence alone does not establish that metaphysics.
claims.primaryQuestion: What metaphysical interpretation might make the orientation landscape intelligible?
claims.strongestCase: The Logos tradition offers an unusually integrated account of intelligibility, truthful speech, sacrificial transformation, personhood, and reconciliation.
claims.counterclaim: Comparable integration is available in rival religious or philosophical traditions, and the apparent fit may be created by selecting and Christianizing the orientation vocabulary.
confidenceReducers: Rival metaphysical frameworks explain the same landscape with equal or greater economy.
The interpretation yields no discriminating expectations or transformative differences.
All contrary evidence is redescribed as resistance, idolatry, or incomplete participation.

challenge.statement: Compare the Logos interpretation with at least two serious rival metaphysical interpretations using criteria fixed before comparison.
challenge.requiredResponse: A symmetrical comparison that permits loss, revision, or local defeat.

thirdOrderAudit.makesLegible: A possible unity among intelligibility, correction, sacrifice, personhood, and reconciliation.
thirdOrderAudit.maySuppress: Religious plurality, non-theistic accounts, divine hiddenness, tragedy without reconciliation, and Christian institutional failure.
thirdOrderAudit.authorityEffect: Can convert a philosophical framework into confessional gatekeeping while presenting the move as neutral inference.
thirdOrderAudit.rivalPreserved: Naturalist pragmatism, Buddhist dependent-origination interpretations, and non-Christian theisms.
thirdOrderAudit.subtractionCondition: Downgrade or locally reject the interpretation where rivals outperform it or where it survives only through circular reinterpretation.

relationships.qualification: Attention is one mechanism of disclosure, not the whole of orientation.
Attentional selection may mediate identity defence but does not establish it.
Corrigibility is proposed partly because meaning alone is insufficient; it remains contestable.
Transformation language is shared; no moral entailment follows.
Mythic recurrence may motivate metaphysical inquiry but cannot prove one tradition.
Both concern transformation and truth; neither entails the other.

forbiddenCollapses.reason: Narrative recurrence does not establish moral truth.
Mythic recurrence does not uniquely confirm Christian metaphysics.
Experienced meaning does not guarantee metaphysical truth.
A defensive causal response does not establish that the defended belief is false.

meceAudit.boundedUniverse: The eight claims selected for the first pilot, not all claims in the manuscript.
meceAudit.mutualExclusivityBasis: Each claim has one primary question and one controlling epistemic class. Relationships do not merge their admission criteria.
meceAudit.exhaustivenessWithinPilot: The pilot covers definition, attentional mechanism, identity dynamics, epistemic guardrail, normative correction quality, cultural-symbolic hypothesis, metaethical proposal, and metaphysical interpretation.
knownCoverageGaps: recognition-versus-transformation and the complete correction cycle
the clinical psychology and psychiatry thesis
collective unconscious as a distinct hypothesis
meceAudit.judgement: MECE enough for a pipeline pilot; not MECE for the complete architecture.
